analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and short-term rentals to advertise the full price including all mandatory fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2022 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat with no further action until Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals from advertising a room rate that leaves out mandatory fees such as "resort fees" or "cleaning fees." The advertised price would have to include every required fee (government taxes excluded). The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rule, and violators would face the same penalties as other deceptive-advertising cases under the FTC Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers booking hotel rooms and short-term rentals. They would see the true total cost of a stay up front instead of discovering mandatory resort or cleaning fees late in the booking process, and could comparison-shop across hotels on an apples-to-apples basis.

how_it_helps.text: Advertising a lodging rate without all required fees would be prohibited, so the price a shopper sees first would include mandatory resort, cleaning, and facility fees (government taxes excluded).
The Federal Trade Commission could enforce the ban with its existing deceptive-practices powers, including penalties, and could write rules to carry it out.
State attorneys general and other authorized state officials could sue on behalf of their residents, giving travelers enforcement even if the FTC did not act.

The bill's findings cite FTC research showing that splitting the room rate from the resort fee raises the mental cost of comparison shopping, leading travelers to make less-informed choices and often pay more for a room.

analysis.who_pays: Hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rental operators that rely on mandatory fees disclosed after the advertised rate, and online travel and metasearch platforms that would have to display all-in pricing. Operators would have to fold fee revenue into the headline rate or compete on a genuinely all-in price.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory fees are real revenue for lodging operators; requiring them in the advertised rate could push headline prices higher, which some travelers may perceive as a price increase even though the total cost is unchanged.

The bill adds a new federal advertising rule and enforcement channels (FTC plus state attorneys general), which expands compliance and litigation exposure for lodging businesses, including small inn and short-term-rental hosts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a straightforward one: travelers can see and compare the actual total price of a stay before booking, instead of hunting for fees buried later in the process. The costs are real but modest, mostly compliance work for lodging operators and platforms and possibly higher-looking headline rates that reflect the same total cost. On balance the bill shifts information power from sellers to buyers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on July 1, 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Represent Eddie Bernice Johnson of Texas introduced the Hotel Advertising Transparency Act of 2022 on July 1, 2022, joined by Representative Trahan, with one cosponsor recorded.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lodging operators and booking platforms that profit from advertising a low base rate and adding mandatory fees later are better off, because the rule never took effect and travelers continued to see fee-separated pricing.

for.name: Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 1, 2022, requiring all-in lodging advertising.

for.name: Rep. Trahan
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor consideration — for the remaining six months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats, but no other members weighed in and no vote was ever held, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested.

industries.note: Many operators advertise a base rate and add mandatory resort, cleaning, or facility fees later in booking; the bill would force that fee revenue into the all-in advertised price or eliminate it. Their gain from fee-separated pricing comes directly out of travelers' ability to know the real cost.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and metasearch platforms
industries.note: The advertising ban explicitly covers third-party distribution and metasearch referrals, so booking sites would have to display all-in prices. Fee-separated displays let platforms advertise lower headline prices than the true total.
